Yes, New York City is sinking at an average rate of 1 to 2 millimeters per year, with some specific areas subsiding up to 4 to 5 millimeters annually. This gradual sinking, combined with rising global sea levels, makes the city increasingly vulnerable to flooding and storm surges. 

Forbes
 +2
The sinking—known technically as land subsidence—is driven by a combination of natural processes and human impacts: 
The Weight of the City: The sheer mass of New York's over one million buildings (weighing roughly 1.68 trillion pounds) presses down on the softer, shifting soils beneath the city.
Natural Geological Shifts: Thousands of years ago, a massive ice sheet covered parts of North America, pushing the edges of the land slightly upward. Now that the ice is gone, that land is slowly readjusting and sinking back down in a process called post-glacial rebound.
Soil and Water: Areas built on soft sediment, artificial fill, or groundwater extraction zones are more prone to uneven compression and faster subsidence rates. 

NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) (.gov)
 +5
Where is it happening fastest?
While the whole city is affected, satellite data pinpointed specific locations sinking at faster rates, including LaGuardia Airport and parts of Queens. These areas are monitored closely as researchers warn that ground motion could impact critical transportation infrastructure over time.
